Surah Ibrahim is Meccan, and it has fifty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book⦆ — that is, it is a Book. ﴿We have sent it down to you that you may bring mankind⦆ — by your calling them to what it contains. ﴿out of darkness⦆ — out of the kinds of misguidance — ﴿into light⦆ — into guidance. ﴿by the permission of their Lord⦆ — by His granting success and facilitation. This is a metaphorical use, borrowed from "permission" (idhn), which is the facilitation of a barrier. The phrase "by the permission of their Lord" is a complement (ṣilah) related to ﴿to bring⦆, or it is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal) of its subject or of its object. ﴿To the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy⦆ — this is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿into light⦆, either by repeating the governing verb, or it is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf), as if it were an answer to someone asking about it. The attribution of "path" to Allah, exalted is He, is either because He is its destination, or because He is the one who makes it manifest. The specification of the two attributes serves to alert that whoever travels it will not be humiliated, and whoever seeks it will not be disappointed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 2–3:

﴿Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ According to the reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, it is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). Or, ﴿Allah﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and "alladhi" (Whom) is its attribute. According to the reading of the rest [of the Readers], it is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿al-ʿAziz﴾ (the Mighty), because it functions like a proper name (ʿilm) due to its being exclusively for the worshipped God in truth. ﴿And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment.﴾ This is a threat for those who disbelieve in the Book and do not, through it, come out from the darknesses into the light. "Al-waylu" (woe) is the opposite of "al-wa'l," which means salvation. Its original form is the accusative (nasb), because it is a verbal noun (masdar), except that no verb has been derived from it; but it was made nominative (raf') to convey permanence.

﴿Those who prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾ choose it over it. For whoever chooses something must seek, from himself, that it be more beloved to him than anything else. ﴿And who bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ by hindering people from faith. It has been read "wa-yusaddūna" (and they cause to be barred), from "asadda-hu," which is transmitted from "sadda sudūdan" when one turns away; and it is not eloquent, because "sadda" has an alternative to the complication of transitivity by the hamzah.

﴿And they seek to make it crooked﴾ meaning they seek for it deviation and inclination away from the truth, in order to find fault with it. The preposition has been omitted and the verb has been connected to the pronoun. The relative clause with its complement may be in the genitive as an attribute of the disbelievers, or in the accusative as a dispraise (dhamm), or in the nominative, either as its predicate or as a subject with a predicate. ﴿Those are in far-off error.﴾ That is, they strayed from the truth and fell far from it by great distances. Distance (bu'd) in reality belongs to the one who is astray, so it was attributed to his action for emphasis; or it was attributed to the matter by which the error occurs because of its connection to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 4:

﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people﴾, that is, except in the dialect (lughah) of his people, the one he is from and among whom he was raised. ﴿So that he might make clear to them﴾ what they were commanded, so that they would understand it from him with ease and speed, and then they would transmit it and translate it to others, for they are the people most worthy of him calling them and most deserving of him warning them. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to warn his closest kin first. Had a book been revealed upon the tongues of one sent to diverse nations, that would have been distinguished by a kind of inimitability (i'jaz), but it would have led to discord in the word (ikhtilaf al-kalimah) and the loss of the merit of striving (ijtihad) in learning the words, their meanings, and the sciences branching from them, and to the wearing down of minds and the exertion of souls, which are among the acts of nearness that merit abundant reward.

It has been read as "bi-lusuni" (بِلُسُنِ), which is a dialect form of the same word, like "risha" and "riyash" (feathers). Also "lusun" with two dammas, and with a damma and a sukun, as a plural, like "umud" and "umd" (pillars). It has also been said that the pronoun in "qawmihi" refers to Muhammad ﷺ, and that God revealed all the books in Arabic, then Jibril (peace be upon him) translated them, or that every prophet spoke the language of those to whom he was sent. But this is not correct, and His saying refutes it: ﴿So that he might make clear to them﴾, for the pronoun refers to the people, and the Torah, the Gospel and the like were not revealed to make things clear to the Arabs.

﴿So Allah leads astray whom He wills﴾, that is, He forsakes him from faith. ﴿And guides whom He wills﴾ by granting him success (tawfiq) in it.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, so He is not overcome in His will. ﴿The Wise﴾, who does not lead astray nor guide except for a wisdom.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 5:

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs﴾: meaning the hand and the staff, and the rest of his miracles. ﴿That bring your people out of darknesses into light﴾: here "an" (أنْ) is interpreted as "i.e." (أي), since sending (al-irsal) carries the sense of saying (al-qawl); or it is "an" meaning "that," since verb forms are alike in indicating the verbal noun, so it is permissible to connect to them the particle "an" (أنِ) which governs the subjunctive (al-nasibah). ﴿And remind them of the Days of Allah﴾: that is, of His events that befell the earlier nations, and the Days of the Arabs were their wars. It has also been said: of His blessings and His trials. ﴿Surely in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾: one who is patient under His trials and thankful for His blessings, for when he hears what was sent down concerning those before him of trials, and what was poured upon them of blessings, he takes heed and becomes alert to what is incumbent upon him of patience and gratitude. It has also been said that what is meant is every believer, and He expressed it thus only to draw attention to the fact that patience and gratitude are the hallmark of the believer.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 6:

﴿And [remember] when Musa said to his people: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you when He delivered you from the people of Fir'awn (Pharaoh)."﴾ That is: remember His favour upon you at the time of His delivering you. It is permissible for it to be governed by ﴿upon you﴾, if it is taken as a stable (predicate) complement and not as a relative complement of "favour"; and that is when by "favour" is meant the gift itself rather than the bestowals. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute for "the favour of Allah," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). ﴿They inflicted upon you the worst of torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women﴾ are circumstantial clauses (ahwal) relating to "the people of Fir'awn," or to the pronoun of the addressees. The meaning of "torment" here differs from its meaning in surah al-Baqarah and surah al-A'raf, because there it is explained as slaughter and killing, and slaughter is coordinated with it (as a separate item) here. It is either the genus of torment, or their enslavement, or their being made to perform arduous labours. ﴿And in that﴾ (is a trial), insofar as it was by Allah's empowering them and granting them respite in it. ﴿was a great trial from your Lord﴾: a test from Him. It is also permissible for the demonstrative to refer to the deliverance, with "trial" meaning favour.

And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ also from the speech of Musa (ﷺ). *Ta'adhdhana* is in the sense of *adhana*, like *tawa'ada* and *awda'a* (both meaning "to threaten"), except that it is more emphatic, because the *tafa''ala* form (the pattern of *ta'adhdhana*) carries the sense of effort and intensification.

﴿If you are thankful﴾ O Children of Israel, for what I have bestowed upon you, such as deliverance and other blessings, by faith and righteous action. ﴿I will surely increase you﴾ in blessing upon blessing. ﴿But if you disbelieve﴾ in what I have bestowed upon you, ﴿indeed My punishment is severe﴾, so I will punish you for ingratitude with a severe punishment. It is the custom of the Most Generous of the generous to state the promise explicitly and to allude to the threat. The clause is either a quoted speech of an implied verb of saying, or the object of ﴿ta'adhdhana﴾, on the basis that it takes the place of "qala" (he said), since it is a kind of saying.

﴿And Musa said: If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on the earth, all together﴾ of the two species (jinn and humankind). ﴿Indeed Allah is Free of need﴾ from your gratitude, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, deserving of praise in His essence, praised by the angels, and the particles of created things speak of His blessing. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 9:

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud?﴾ It is either part of the speech of Musa (peace be upon him), or a new statement begun by Allah. ﴿And those after them, none knows them but Allah.﴾ This is a sentence placed as an interjection (i'tirad, a parenthetical clause inserted within the discourse). Alternatively, ﴿those after them﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes it, and ﴿none knows them﴾ is an interjection. The meaning is that, because of their great number, none knows their count but Allah. For this reason Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The genealogists have lied." ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they put their hands into their mouths.﴾ That is, they bit them out of rage at what the messengers (peace be upon them) brought, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage.﴾ Or they placed them upon their mouths out of amazement at him, or in mockery of him, like one overcome by laughter. Or it was to silence the prophets (peace be upon them) and to command them to close their mouths. Or they pointed with them to their tongues, and to what their tongues uttered of their saying: ﴿Indeed we disbelieve,﴾ as an indication that they have no answer other than this. Or they put them into the mouths of the prophets, preventing them from speaking. On this view, it may be a figurative expression (tamthil, an image drawn for the sake of illustration). It has also been said that "al-aydi" (the hands) is in the sense of "al-ayadi" (the favours/blessings), meaning: they returned the prophets' ayadi, which are their admonitions and the wisdom and laws revealed to them, into their own mouths. For when they denied these and did not accept them, it is as though they returned them to the place from which they had come. ﴿And they said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent,﴾ according to your claim. ﴿And indeed we are in doubt about that to which you invite us,﴾ of faith. It is also read "tad'unana" with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters). ﴿Disquieting (murib),﴾ causing unease, or possessing unease, which is restlessness of the soul and the failure to be at peace with a thing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 10:

﴿Their messengers said: "Is there doubt about God, Originator of the heavens and the earth?"﴾ The interrogative particle (hamzat al-inkar, the particle of denial) has been placed upon the adverbial phrase (al-zarf, here "about God"), because the discussion concerns that about which doubt is held, not doubt itself. That is: "We only call you to God, and He does not admit of doubt, due to the abundance of proofs and the manifestness of their indication of Him." They pointed to this by their saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, which is either a qualifier (sifah) or an appositive (badal), and "doubt" is raised by the adverbial phrase. ﴿He calls you﴾ to belief in His sending us. ﴿that He may forgive you﴾, or that He may call you to forgiveness, like your saying: "I called him to help me," with the object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) placed in the position of the direct object (maf'ul bihi). ﴿some of your sins﴾: some of your sins, which are those between you and God the Exalted, for Islam erases these, but not wrongs against people (al-mazalim). It has been said that "min" (some of) was used in addressing the disbelievers, but not the believers, throughout the Qur'an, to distinguish between the two forms of address. The likely meaning of this is that forgiveness, wherever it comes in address to disbelievers, is conditioned upon faith, and wherever it comes in address to believers, it is accompanied by obedience, abstention from sins, and the like, so it encompasses leaving aside wrongs against people. ﴿and defer you to a named term﴾: until a time that God the Exalted has named and made the last of your lifespans. ﴿They said: "You are only mortals like us"﴾: you have no superiority over us, so why are you singled out for prophethood to the exclusion of us? And had God willed to send messengers to mankind, He would have sent them from a superior kind. ﴿You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship﴾ by this claim. ﴿Then bring us a manifest authority﴾: which demonstrates your superiority and your deservingness of this distinction, or which demonstrates the soundness of your claim to prophethood. It is as though they did not consider what they had been brought of clear signs and proofs, and proposed to them another sign out of obstinacy and contentiousness.

(p-195) ﴿They said to them: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour on whomever He wills of His servants."﴾ They acknowledged their sharing with them in the species, and made the cause for their being singled out for prophethood the grace and bounty of God upon them. In this is evidence that prophethood is a bestowed gift, and that the preference of some possible things over others is by the will of God Most High. ﴿It was not for us to bring you an authority except by the leave of God.﴾ That is: bringing signs is not up to us, nor is it within our power to do so independently, so that we could bring what you have demanded; rather it is a matter that depends on the will of God Most High, who singles out each prophet with a certain kind of sign. ﴿And upon God let the believers rely.﴾ That is: let us rely upon Him in patience over your opposition and hostility. They generalized the command as a motto, with what necessitates reliance, and by it they intended themselves primarily. Do you not see His saying, Most High: ﴿And why should we not rely upon God?﴾ That is: what excuse do we have for not relying upon Him? ﴿And He has guided us to our ways.﴾ The ways by which we know Him and know that all affairs are in His hand. Abu 'Amr recited with the light (takhfif) form here and in "al-'Ankabut." ﴿And we will surely bear patiently what you have harmed us with.﴾ This is the answer to an implied oath, by which they affirmed their reliance and their indifference to what the unbelievers inflicted upon them. ﴿And upon God let those who rely [upon Him] rely.﴾ That is: let those who rely remain steadfast in what they have newly undertaken of their reliance, which was caused by their faith.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 14, verses 13–14:

﴿And those who disbelieved said to their messengers, "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion."﴾ They swore that one of the two matters would occur: either their expulsion of the messengers or the messengers' return to their religion. The "return" is used in the sense of "becoming," because they had never been upon their religion at all. It is also possible that the address is to every messenger and those who believed with him, so the group was given precedence over the singular. ﴿Then their Lord revealed to them﴾, that is, to their messengers: ﴿"We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ This is either by implying a verb of saying (*qawl*), or by treating the revelation (*iyha'*) as if it were speech, since it is a type of it.

﴿"And We will surely settle you in the land after them."﴾ That is, their land and their dwellings, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern parts of the earth and its western parts﴾ (7:137). It was also read as *layuhlikanna* (﻿ليُهْلِكَنَّ) and *laywsakinannakum* (﻿وليُسْكِنَنَّكم) with the *ya'* (third person), taking into account that the verb *awha* (﻿أوحى) is the subject, as in your saying, "Zayd swore that he would surely go out" (*aqsama Zaydun layakhrujanna*). ﴿That﴾ is a reference to what was revealed, namely the destruction of the wrongdoers and the settling of the believers. ﴿For him who fears My standing (*maqami*)﴾, that is, My station (*mawqifi*), which is the place where servants stand for judgment on the Day of Resurrection; or it means My standing over him and My preservation of his deeds. It is also said that *maqam* here is superfluous (*muqhamun*).

﴿And fears My threat (*wa'id*)﴾, that is, My threat of punishment, or My promised punishment for the disbelievers.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 14, verses 15–17:**

﴿And they sought victory﴾: they asked God for victory over their enemies, or for judgment between them and their enemies, from *al-fataha* (judgment), as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth﴾. It is conjoined (*ma'tuf*, grammatically coordinated) with ﴿so He revealed﴾, and the pronoun refers to the Prophets, upon them be blessings and peace. It was also said that it refers to the disbelievers, and it was said that it refers to both parties, for all of them asked Him to grant victory to the one who is right and to destroy the one who is false. It was also recited with the imperative form, coordinated with *la-yuhlikanna* ("He will surely destroy"). ﴿And every obstinate tyrant failed﴾: that is, He opened [victory] for them, so the believers prospered, and every arrogant tyrant (*'at*, transgressor), proud toward God, opposed to the truth, did not prosper. The sense of failure (*al-khaybah*), when the seeking of victory is by the disbelievers, or by both parties, is more fitting.

﴿Before him is Hell﴾: that is, before him, for he is kept under watch by it, standing at its edge in this world, and he will be sent to it in the Hereafter. It was said: "from behind his life," and its literal meaning is "what is hidden from you." ﴿And he will be given to drink of water﴾ is coordinated (*'utifa*) with an elided element whose sense is: "Before him is Hell, where he will be cast, and he will be given to drink of water." ﴿Of pus﴾ is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*, a clarifying appositive) to *ma'* ("water"), and it is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire.

﴿He will gulp it﴾: he will strain himself to swallow it, and this is an attribute of *ma'* ("water"), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yusqa* ("he will be given to drink"). ﴿And he almost cannot swallow it﴾: he will not come close to swallowing it, so how could he swallow it? Rather, it will choke him, and so his punishment will be prolonged. *Al-sawgh* ("swallowing") is the passage of a drink down the throat with ease and the soul's acceptance of it. ﴿And death will come to him from every place﴾: that is, its causes, from the severities, will surround him from all directions. It was also said: "from every place of his body, even from the roots of his hair and the tips of his toes." ﴿Yet he will not die﴾, so that he might find rest. ﴿And before him﴾: that is, from before him. ﴿A harsh punishment﴾: that is, he will face at every moment a punishment harsher than that in which he is. It was said that it is abiding eternally in the Fire, and it was said that it is the withholding of breath.

It was also said that the verse is detached from the account of the Messengers and was revealed concerning the people of Makkah, who sought the "victory," which is rain, during the years of drought that God sent upon them through the supplication of His Messenger. He disappointed their hope, so He did not give them water, and He promised that He would give them drink in Hell in place of their watering, namely the pus of the people of the Fire.

The sense of failure (*al-khaybah*), when the seeking of victory is by the disbelievers, or by both parties, is more fitting.

﴿Before him is Hell﴾: that is, before him, for he is kept under watch by it, standing at its edge in this world, and he will be sent to it in the Hereafter. It was said: "from behind his life," and its literal meaning is "what is hidden from you." ﴿And he will be given to drink of water﴾ is coordinated (*'utifa*) with an elided element whose sense is: "Before him is Hell, where he will be cast, and he will be given to drink of water." ﴿Of pus﴾ is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*, a clarifying appositive) to *ma'* ("water"), and it is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire.

﴿He will gulp it﴾: he will strain himself to swallow it, and this is an attribute of *ma'* ("water"), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yusqa* ("he will be given to drink"). ﴿And he almost cannot swallow it﴾: he will not come close to swallowing it, so how could he swallow it? Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 18:

﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: "in what is recited to you, is their description, which is a likeness in its strangeness." Or [the predicate is] his saying ﴿their deeds are like ashes﴾, and this, according to the first view, is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) explaining their likeness. It has been said that ﴿their deeds﴾ is an apposition (badal) to ﴿likeness﴾, and the predicate is ﴿like ashes﴾.

﴿The wind blows violently upon it﴾: it carries it away and hastens its removal. Nafi' read "al-Riyah" (the winds).

﴿On a stormy day﴾: al-'asf is the intensification of the wind. Its time has been described with it for emphasis, as in the saying of people: "its day is fasting and its night is standing (in prayer)." He likened their good works, such as charity, maintaining ties of kinship, relieving the distressed, freeing slaves, and similar noble deeds, in their being nullified and dispersed as scattered dust (habaan manthuran), because they were built on no foundation of knowledge of God Most High and were not directed towards Him. Or [it means] their deeds offered to idols are like ashes which the stormy wind has scattered.

﴿They have no power﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿over what they have earned﴾ of their deeds ﴿[as] anything﴾, because of its nullification, so they see no trace of reward from it; and this is the summation (fadhlaka) of the likeness.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to their misguidance, together with their assumption that they are doing good. ﴿That is the far-reaching error﴾, for it is the utmost distance from the path of truth.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verses 19–20:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community (ummah). It has also been said that it is addressed to each one of the disbelievers, by way of shifting the address (al-talwin). ﴿That God created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ — with wisdom and in the manner that befits their being created. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "khaliq al-samawat" (the Creator of the heavens). ﴿If He wills, He will remove you and bring a new creation﴾ — He will annihilate you and create another creation in your place. He arranged this upon His being the Creator of the heavens and the earth, as a proof of it: for whoever created their roots (usul) and what their creation depends upon, then brought them into being through the alteration of forms and the changing of natures, is able to replace them with another creation, and this is not impossible for Him, as He said: ﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾ — not unattainable or hard, for He is capable in His very essence, and there is no specificity to Him regarding one object of power over another. Whoever has this quality is worthy to be believed in and worshipped, hoping for His reward and fearing His punishment on the Day of Recompense.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verses 19–20:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community (ummah). It has also been said that it is addressed to each one of the disbelievers, by way of shifting the address (al-talwin). ﴿That God created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ — with wisdom and in the manner that befits their being created. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "khaliq al-samawat" (the Creator of the heavens). ﴿If He wills, He will remove you and bring a new creation﴾ — He will annihilate you and create another creation in your place. He arranged this upon His being the Creator of the heavens and the earth, as a proof of it: for whoever created their roots (usul) and what their creation depends upon, then brought them into being through the alteration of forms and the changing of natures, is able to replace them with another creation, and this is not impossible for Him, as He said: ﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾ — not unattainable or hard, for He is capable in His very essence, and there is no specificity to Him regarding one object of power over another. Whoever has this quality is worthy to be believed in and worshipped, hoping for His reward and fearing His punishment on the Day of Recompense.

﴿And they will come forth before Allah, all of them﴾: that is, they will come forth from their graves on the Day of Resurrection, to the command of Allah, the Exalted, and to His reckoning. Or, [it means] "before Allah" according to their assumption, for they used to conceal the commission of vile deeds and think that they were hidden from Allah, the Exalted. When the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be exposed before Allah, the Exalted, in their own estimation. The verb is expressed in the past tense only to affirm that it will certainly occur.

﴿Then the weak﴾, meaning the followers, plural of ḍaʿīf (weak). By this he means those weak in judgment (ḍiʿāf al-ra'y). It is written with a waw (وَ) in the script, following the pronunciation of one who emphasizes the alif before the hamza and inclines it toward the waw.

﴿will say to those who were arrogant﴾, meaning to their leaders who led them astray and misled them.

﴿Indeed, we were following you﴾, in denying the messengers and turning away from their advice. Tabaʿan is the plural of tābiʿ (follower), like ghāʾib and ghuyyab (absent). Or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) described by it for emphasis, or [it is] by supposing an omitted genitive construction (muḍāf).

﴿So will you avail us anything against the punishment of Allah?﴾, meaning, will you ward off from us [any part of] it?

﴿anything﴾ (min shayʾ): the first min (مِن) is explanatory (lil-bayān) and occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The second min is partitive (lil-tabʿīḍ) and occupies the position of the object, meaning some part of the thing which is the punishment of Allah. It is permissible that both be partitive, meaning some part of a thing which is part of the punishment of Allah. The i'rāb (grammatical analysis) is what has preceded. It is also possible that the first (min) is the object and the second is a verbal noun, meaning: will you avert some of the punishment with some degree of averting?

﴿They will say﴾, that is, those who were arrogant, in response to the reproach of the followers and as an apology for what they did to them.

﴿Had Allah guided us﴾ to faith and granted us success in it.

﴿we would have guided you﴾. But we went astray, so we led you astray, meaning we chose for you what we chose for ourselves. Or [it means]: had Allah guided us to the path of salvation from the punishment, we would have guided you and made you independent of it, just as we exposed you to it; but the path of escape was closed to us.

﴿It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently﴾, meaning both are equal for us, lamenting and enduring patiently.

﴿We have no place of escape﴾, meaning refuge and a way of flight from the punishment. It is from al-ḥays, which is deviating by way of flight. It may be a place, like mabīt (a place of spending the night), or a verbal noun, like maghīb (a setting). It is also permissible that the phrase ﴿It is all the same for us﴾ is part of the speech of both groups. This is supported by what has been narrated: they say, "Come, let us lament," and they lament for five hundred years, but it does not benefit them. Then they say, "Come, let us endure patiently," and they endure patiently in the same way, and then they say, ﴿It is all the same for us﴾.

﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided﴾, that is, when it has been judged, completed, and finished, and the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, as an orator among the wretched of both jinn and humankind. ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth﴾, a promise that is due from Him to be fulfilled, or a promise that He has fulfilled, namely the promise of resurrection and recompense. ﴿And I promised you﴾ the promise of falsehood, which is that there is no resurrection and no reckoning, and that if there were, the idols would intercede for you. ﴿But I broke it to you﴾: he made the manifestation of the breaking of His promise equivalent to His breaking it. ﴿And I had no authority over you﴾, no power, so that I would compel you to disbelief and sins. ﴿Except that I called you﴾, meaning only my calling you to them through my enticement. This is not of the kind of authority, but it is in the manner of their saying: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow." It is also permissible that the exception be disjunctive (munqati', i.e., not from the same category).

﴿So you responded to me﴾, you hastened to answer me. ﴿So do not blame me﴾ for my whispering, for one who openly declares enmity is not blamed for such things. ﴿But blame yourselves﴾, since you obeyed me when I called you, and you did not obey your Lord when He called you. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that affirms human free will and the createdness of the Qur'an) argued with the like of these verses for the independence of the servant in his actions, but there is nothing in them that indicates this, since for their validity it suffices that the servant's power have some role in his act, which is the acquisition (kasb) that our companions (the Ash'arites) affirm.

﴿I cannot help you﴾, meaning I cannot rescue you from the punishment. ﴿Nor can you help me﴾, meaning you cannot rescue me. Hamzah (a Qur'anic reader) read it with a kasrah on the ya' (the pronominal ya', i.e., "bi-muṣrikhiyya") according to the original form for meeting two unvowelled letters. This is an original form that is rejected in such a case, because it involves the gathering of two ya's and three kasrahs, while the vowel of the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah) is fatha. So if it is not given a kasrah when preceded by an alif, it is even more fitting that it not be given a kasrah when preceded by a ya'. Or it is according to the dialect of those who add a ya' after the ya' of possession, treating it like the ha' and kaf in "ḍaraba-hu" ("he struck him") and "a'ṭai-tu-ka-hu" ("I gave it to you"), and the ya' is omitted, being satisfied with the kasrah.

﴿Indeed, I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah before﴾. "Ma" is either a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), and "min" is connected to "ashraktumūnī," meaning: I disbelieve today in your associating me [with Allah] from before this day, i.e., in the world, in the sense that I disowned it and denounced it, like His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will disown your associating [of them]﴾. Or "ma" is a relative pronoun in the sense of "min" as in the phrase "Glory be to Him who subjected these to us," and "min" is connected to "kafartu," meaning: I disbelieved in the One whom you made a partner with Him, who is Allah the Exalted, by your obedience to me in what I called you to of worshipping idols and other things before your association [of partners], when I rejected His command to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him. And "ashraka" is transitive, derived from "sharaktu Zayd[an]," to make it transitive to a second object.

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment﴾. This is either the conclusion of his speech, or the beginning of a speech from Allah, the Exalted. In relating the likes of this there is gentle kindness for the listeners (p-198) and an awakening for them, so that they may take account of themselves and reflect upon their outcomes.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 23:

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be made to enter gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord﴾. "By the permission of God Most High" means by His leave and command. Those who are made to enter are the angels. It has been read as "وأدْخَلَ" (wa-adkhala, "and He caused to enter") in the first-person form of speech (al-taka!lum), in which case the phrase ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾ is connected to the phrase ﴿their greeting therein is peace﴾, meaning: the angels greet them therein with peace, by the permission of their Lord.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verses 24–25:

﴿Have you not considered how Allah has set forth a parable?﴾ "Kayfa" (how) here is in the accusative because it is governed by "i'tamadahu" (He made it) and "wada'ahu" (He placed it). ﴿A good word is like a good tree﴾ That is, He made a good word like a good tree, and this is an explanation of His saying ﴿has set forth a parable﴾. It is permissible for ﴿a word﴾ to be a substitute (badal) for ﴿a parable﴾, with ﴿like a tree﴾ being its description, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is like a tree." It is also permissible for it to be the first of the two objects of "darraba" (set forth), treating it as "ja'ala" (made). It has also been read in the nominative (marfu') as a beginning (mubtada'). ﴿Its root is firmly fixed﴾ in the earth, striking its roots into it. ﴿And its branches﴾ and its top ﴿are in the sky﴾. It is also permissible that it means "wa furu'uha" (its branches), that is, its offshoots, with the singular noun used for the genus, since the genitive construction gives it the sense of comprehensiveness.

It was also read "thabitun asluha" (firm is its root), and the first reading is on its original form; for this reason it has been said that it is stronger, though the second is probably more eloquent.

﴿It gives its fruit﴾ it yields its produce. ﴿Every season﴾ which Allah, exalted is He, has appointed for its bearing fruit. ﴿By the permission of its Lord﴾ by the will of its Creator and His bringing it into being. ﴿And Allah sets forth parables for the people that they may take heed﴾ because in setting them forth there is greater understanding and reminder, for it is a depiction of meanings and a bringing of them close to the senses.

(Qur'an 14:26) "And the likeness of an evil word is that of an evil tree" [kalimatin khabitha kashajaratin khabitha] — "like an evil tree that has been uprooted from above the earth (ijtuththat), its whole trunk pulled out entirely, having no stability (qarar)."

Al-Baydawi: "Ijtuththat" means it was utterly uprooted and its trunk (juththa) was taken out completely. "From above the earth" because its roots are close to the surface. "Having no stability" means it has no firm footing.

There is a difference of opinion regarding the "word" and the "tree." The good word has been explained as the word of tawhid (the declaration of divine oneness), the call of Islam, and the Qur'an; and the evil word as associating partners with God (shirk), calling to disbelief, and denying the truth. It is likely that what is intended by both is everything that includes these: the good word is whatever expresses a truth or calls to righteousness, and the evil word is whatever runs contrary to that.

The good tree has been explained as the date palm (al-nakhla). This is also narrated as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report, and as a tree in Paradise. The evil tree has been explained as the colocynth (al-hanzala) and dodder (al-kashuth). It is likely that what is intended by both of these is also everything that includes this.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 27:

﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾, which is firm through proof in their estimation and has taken root in their hearts, ﴿in the life of this world﴾, so they do not waver when they are tested in their religion, like Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both, and Jirjis (Jirjis, St. George), and Shamʿun (Shamʿun, Simon), and those whom the people of the trench (ashab al-ukhdud) tested. ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾, so they do not falter when they are asked about their belief at the place of standing (al-mawqif), and the terrors of the Day of Resurrection do not bewilder them.

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the taking of the soul of the believer and said: Then his soul is returned to his body, and two angels come to him and seat him in his grave and say to him: Who is your Lord? What is your religion? And who is your Prophet? So he says: My Lord is Allah, my religion is Islam, and my Prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ). Then a caller calls from the heaven: My servant has spoken the truth. That is His saying: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾.

﴿And Allah leads the wrongdoers astray﴾, those who wronged themselves by confining themselves to blind imitation (taqlid), so they are not guided to the truth and do not remain steadfast in the times of trial. ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾, of keeping some firm and leading others astray, without anyone objecting to Him.

Have you not seen those who exchanged the favour of Allah for ingratitude? That is, the thanks due for His favour, by putting ingratitude in its place. Or they exchanged the favour itself for disbelief. When they disbelieved in it, it was taken away from them, so they became abandoning it and acquiring disbelief in its place, like the people of Makkah. Allah created them, settled them in His sanctuary, made them the custodians of His House, widened for them the doors of His provision, and honoured them with Muhammad (ﷺ). They denied that, so they were struck with famine for seven years, were taken captive and killed on the day of Badr, and became humbled. Thus they remained deprived of the favour and described with disbelief. It is also reported from ʿUmar and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are "the two most wicked families of Quraysh: the Banu al-Mughirah and the Banu Umayyah. As for the Banu al-Mughirah, you were sufficed against them on the day of Badr, and as for the Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time."

﴿And caused their people to alight﴾: their followers in disbelief. ﴿the abode of ruin﴾: the abode of destruction, by their leading them to disbelief.

Or it explains an implied verb governing ﴿Hell﴾. ﴿And wretched is the place of settlement﴾: that is, and wretched is the place of abode, Hell.

﴿And they set up rivals to Allah in order to mislead [others] from His way﴾, which is tawhid (monotheism, the affirmation of God's oneness). Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ruways from Yaʿqub read the verb ﴿to mislead﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ. Misguidance or misleading was not their aim in taking rivals, but since it was its consequence, it was treated as though it were the aim. ﴿Say: Enjoy yourselves﴾ with your desires, or with the worship of idols, for they belong to the category of desires one enjoys. The use of the imperative form in the threat indicates that what is threatened is treated as though it were willed, since it leads to what is threatened, and that both matters are certain to happen. For this reason He gave the reason for it in His words: ﴿for your destination is the Fire﴾, and that the addressees, being immersed in it, are treated as those commanded by an obeyed commander.

Or it explains an implied verb governing ﴿Hell﴾. ﴿And wretched is the place of settlement﴾: that is, and wretched is the place of abode, Hell.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 31:

﴿Say to My servants who have believed﴾ He specified them by the (possessive) attribution (of "servants") to honour them and to draw attention to the fact that they are the ones who uphold the rights of servanthood. The object of ﴿Say﴾ is omitted, indicated by its answer (the jussive that follows): that is, "Say to My servants who have believed: Establish the prayer and spend." ﴿That they establish the prayer and spend of what We have provided for them﴾. This therefore serves as a notice that, owing to their great obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ), their actions never separate from his command, and that he is like the cause that necessitates it. It is also permissible to take both verbs as preceded by the imperative particle (lam al-amr, "let"), so that saying can be connected to both of them. This is good here but was not good in the saying of the poet:

"Muhammad, let every soul ransom itself (with you), / when you fear some calamity (tabal)."

(This is not good there) because the word "say" (qul) does not indicate it. It was also said that both are answers to aqimu and anfiqu, standing in their place, but this is weak, because there must be a difference between the conditional and its answer, and because a direct command addressed to the second person is not answered with the third-person form when the doer is one.

﴿Secretly and openly﴾: both are in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (meaning the spending of secrecy and openness), or as a circumstantial accusative (meaning those who are in secrecy and openness), or as an adverbial accusative of time (meaning the times of secrecy and openness). The better course is to make obligatory giving public and to conceal voluntary giving.

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trading﴾, so that the negligent may buy what will make up for his shortcoming, or ransom himself by it. ﴿Nor friendship﴾: that is, no companionship, so that a friend may intercede for you. Or (the meaning is): before there comes a Day in which there is no benefit from trade or from friendship, and in which benefit comes only from spending for the sake of Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read both (la bay'un and la khilalun) with a fatha, as a general negation.

(p-200)

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾: *Allah* is the *mubtada'* (subject) and *alladhi khalaqa* is the *khabar* (predicate).

﴿And sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾: *rizqan* (provision) is the *maf'ul* (object) of *akhraja*. ﴿Of the fruits﴾ is a *bayan* (explanatory elaboration) of it and also a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) of it. It is possible that this is reversed. It is also permissible that *rizqan* is meant as a verbal noun (*masdar*), in which case it is in the accusative as an *'illa* (causal accusative, "for the sake of provision"), or that it is a *masdar* because *akhraja* carries the meaning of *razaqa* (provided). The provision (*rizq*) you live by includes both what is eaten and what is worn.

﴿And subjected for you the ships to run upon the sea by His command﴾, that is, by His will, to wherever you direct them.

﴿And subjected for you the rivers﴾, making them prepared for your benefit and your use. It has been said that the subjugation of these things is a teaching of how to make use of them.

﴿And subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant﴾: they persevere in their motion and their giving of light and in the maintenance of what they sustain among created beings.

﴿And subjected for you the night and the day﴾: they alternate for your rest and your livelihood.

﴿And gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾: that is, some of everything you asked of Him. The meaning is: of every thing you asked Him for, He gave you some. The existing of each kind is only a part of what lies within the power of Allah, the Exalted. Perhaps what is meant by ﴿what you asked Him﴾ is what is fitting to be asked, due to the need of people for it, whether or not it was asked. The word *ma* may be a relative pronoun, a descriptive, or a verbal-noun particle, in which case the *masdar* carries the sense of the passive participle (*maf'ul*). It has been read as *min kullin* with tanwin, meaning "and He gave you of every thing what you needed and asked for through the tongue of your state." It is also permissible that *ma* is a negation in the position of a *hal*, meaning "and He gave you of every thing, not as those who ask Him."

﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you will not enumerate it﴾: you cannot confine it, nor are you able to count its kinds, let alone its individual instances, for it is without limit. In this is evidence that the singular noun, when made genitive by an attached noun, conveys totality (*istighraq*).

﴿Indeed, mankind is truly a wrongdoer﴾: he wrongs the favour by neglecting its thanks, or he wrongs himself by exposing himself to deprivation.

﴿Ungrateful﴾: exceedingly ungrateful. It has been said: *zalum* (wrongdoer) in hardship, complaining and despairing; *kaffar* (ungrateful) in ease, hoarding and withholding.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 35–36:

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this land﴾ — the city of Makkah — ﴿secure﴾, possessing security for those who are in it. The difference between this and his words, ﴿make this a secure land﴾, is that what he asks for in the first is the removal of fear from it and making it secure, while in the second it is making it one of the secure lands. ﴿And keep me and my sons﴾ — distance me and them — ﴿far from worshipping idols﴾, and place us on the side away from them. It is also read as «wa-ajnibni» (ﵟوأجنبني), and both forms are according to the dialect of Najd, whereas the people of the Hijaz say jannibni sharrahu (keep its evil away from me). In it is evidence that the infallibility of the prophets is by Allah's granting success (tawfiq) and His protection of them, and that by its apparent meaning it does not extend to his descendants and all of his offspring. Ibn Uyaynah claimed that the children of Isma'il, upon him be peace, did not worship an idol, citing this verse, and that they only had stones which they circumambulated and called the "Dawwar", and said: "The House is a stone, so wherever we set up a stone, it has the same status."

﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray﴾ — therefore I asked You for infallibility and sought refuge in You from their misguidance. The attribution of misguidance to them is by way of causation, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the life of this world deceived them﴾. ﴿Whoever follows me﴾ in my religion ﴿is of me﴾, i.e., is part of me, not separated from me in matters of religion. ﴿And whoever disobeys me — indeed You are Forgiving, Merciful﴾: You are able to forgive him and show mercy to him, either from the outset or after granting him success in repentance. In it is evidence that every sin is something Allah may forgive, even shirk, except that the threat has distinguished it from other than it.

(p-201) "Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring" (that is, some of my offspring, or a portion of my offspring; the object has been omitted, and it refers to Isma'il and those descended from him, since settling him there implies settling them). "In a valley without cultivation" (meaning the valley of Makkah, which is rocky and does not grow crops). "By Your Sacred House" (which You have made sacred by forbidding any violation of it or disrespect toward it; or it has always been venerated and protected, so that tyrants stand in awe of it; or it prevented the Flood from reaching it and so no one could seize it. For this reason it was called ʿAtīq, meaning "freed," that is, freed from domination). If he made this supplication when he first arrived, then he said it with regard to what then existed, or with regard to what it would eventually become.

It is narrated that Hajar belonged to Sarah, may Allah be pleased with her, who gave her to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and she bore him Isma'il, peace be upon him. Sarah became jealous of them, so she begged him to remove them from her presence, and he took them to the land of Makkah. Then Allah caused the spring of Zamzam to gush forth. Then the tribe of Jurhum saw birds there and said, "There are no birds except over water," so they headed toward it and found the two of them with a spring nearby. They said, "Share your water with us, and we will share our milk with you," and she agreed.

"Our Lord, that they may establish the prayer." The lam here is the lam of purpose (lam al-kay), and it is connected to "I have settled." That is: I have settled them in this barren valley, from which there is no place of resort or livelihood, only so that they may establish the prayer by Your Sacred House.

The repetition of the address and its placement in the middle is to signal that this is the primary purpose of settling them there. The aim of the supplication is that Allah grant them success in it.

It has also been said that the lam is the lam of command (lam al-amr), and the meaning is a prayer for them to establish the prayer, as if he were asking them to establish it and asking Allah Most High to grant them success in it. "So make hearts incline toward them from among the people." That is, hearts from among the hearts of people, and "from" (min) here is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ). For this reason it was said that if he had said "hearts of the people," Persia and the Romans would have crowded upon them, and the Jews and Christians would have made pilgrimage to them. Or the "min" is for beginning (lil-ibtidāʾ), as in your saying, "The heart from me is sick," meaning the hearts of certain people.

Hisham read "afʾidatan" with the variant transmission from him, with a yāʾ after the hamzah. It has also been read "āfidatan," which may be an inverted form of "afʾidatan," like ādar for adʾur, or an active participle from afadtu al-riḥlata, meaning when I hasten the journey, that is, a group who hasten toward them. It has also been read "afadatan" with the hamzah dropped for ease, though the proper way is to pronounce it between the hamzah and the vowel (bayna bayn). It may also be from afada. "Swoop toward them" means hasten toward them out of longing and affection. It has been read "tuhwā" in the passive, from ahwā ilayhi ghayrahu (to make someone else incline toward it), and "tahwī" from hawiya yahwī, meaning to love; its construction with "ilā" is because it implies the sense of yearning.

"And provide them with fruits" despite their settling in a valley where nothing grows. "That perhaps they may give thanks" for that blessing. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, answered his supplication and made it a secure sanctuary to which the fruits of everything are brought, to the extent that fruits of spring, summer, and autumn are found there on a single day.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 14, verses 38–39:

﴿Our Lord, You indeed know what we conceal and what we disclose.﴾ He knows our secret as He knows our open matters. The meaning is: You are more knowing of our circumstances and our interests, and more merciful to us, than we are to ourselves. So there is no need for us to request anything, but we call upon You to manifest our servitude (*ubudiyyah*), to express our dependence on Your mercy, and to hasten the attainment of what is with You. It has been said that "what we conceal" refers to the anguish of separation, and "what we disclose" refers to our supplication to You and our reliance upon You. The repetition of the address (*nida'*) is for the sake of intensifying the humble supplication and the seeking of refuge with God Most High. ﴿Nothing is hidden from God on earth or in heaven.﴾ Because He is the Knower by an essential knowledge (*'ilm dhati*) whose relation is equal to every object of knowledge, and "min" here is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*).

﴿All praise is due to God, who has granted me, in old age,﴾ that is, who has granted me while I was old and despaired of children. He restricted the granting to the state of old age to magnify the blessing and to show the favours of God within it. ﴿Ishmael and Isaac.﴾

It is narrated that Ishmael was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Isaac when he was one hundred and twelve years old.

﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.﴾ That is, the One who answers it. From your saying, "The king heard my speech," when he took it into account. It is from the intensive patterns (*abniyat al-mubalaghah*) that operate as a verb, and it is annexed to its object or its subject, with the hearing attributed to the supplication of God Most High figuratively (*'ala al-majaz*). Within it is an indication that he called upon his Lord and asked Him for a child, and He answered him and granted him his request at the very time when despair had set in, so that it would be among the most magnificent and most manifest of blessings.(p-202)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verses 40–41:

﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer﴾, meaning one who maintains it (mu'didan lahā) and is constant in it (muwāẓiban ʿalayhā). ﴿And [make] from my descendants [such]﴾. It is conjoined to the object in ﴿make me﴾. The partitive (al-tab'īd, "some of") is used because he knew, either by Allah's informing him or by inductive observation of His custom among earlier nations, that there would be disbelievers among his descendants. ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾, meaning answer my supplication (wa-istajib duʿāʾī), or accept my worship (wa-taqabbal ʿibādatī).

﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾. It is also read "wa-li-abawayya" (and to my two fathers). The reason for his seeking forgiveness for them has already been discussed. It has been said that by "my two parents" he meant Adam and Eve.

﴿And for the believers on the day the reckoning takes place﴾. "Yaqūmu" (takes place, stands) is a metaphor borrowed from standing over a man, as in their saying: "The war stood on one leg" (qāmat al-ḥarbu ʿalā sāq). Alternatively, the meaning is that his people stand up to it (yaqūmu ilayhi ahluhu), so the object is elided (ḥudhifa al-muḍāf), or its standing is attributed to it figuratively (majāzan).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verses 42–43:

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do.﴾ This is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and its purpose is to strengthen him in what he already holds, namely that He, exalted is He, is aware of their conditions and actions, and nothing hidden is concealed from Him; and it is a warning that He will certainly punish them for their little and their much. Or it is addressed to everyone who imagines His heedlessness, out of ignorance of His attributes and deception by His granting them respite. It has also been said that it is a consolation for the wronged and a threat to the wrongdoer.

﴿Indeed, He only delays them﴾, that is, He delays their punishment. It is also reported from Abu 'Amr with the nun (﴿Nuʾakhkhiruhum﴾).

﴿until a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾, that is, their eyes will stare fixedly on that Day and will not stay still in their places because of the terror of what they see.

﴿Hastening forward﴾, that is, hurrying toward the caller; or advancing with their eyes fixed, not blinking, out of awe and fear. The root of the word is the act of turning toward something. ﴿With their heads raised﴾, that is, lifting them up. ﴿Their gaze will not return to them﴾, rather their eyes remain fixed, not blinking; or their look does not come back to them so that they look at themselves. ﴿And their hearts will be a void﴾, that is, empty of understanding because of extreme bewilderment and astonishment. From this, one says of a fool or a coward that his heart is "hawa'" (void), meaning he has no judgment and no strength. Zuhayr said:

﴿Of the cranes, his breast is hollow (hawa')﴾

It has also been said that it means empty of good, void of truth.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verses 45–46:

﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ through disbelief and sins, like ʿAd and Thamud. The original usage of sakana (to dwell) is to be followed by fi (in), as with qarra (to settle), ghaniya (to abide) and aqama (to reside). It may also be used in the sense of tabwi' (to settle someone in a place), in which case it operates in the same way, as in your saying: sakantu al-dar (I settled the house).

﴿And it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾ through what you witness in their dwellings of the traces of what befell them, and what has reached you through successive reports of their accounts. ﴿And We set forth for you the parables﴾ from their circumstances, meaning: We made clear to you that you are like them in disbelief and in deserving punishment. Or [it means] the descriptions of what they did and what was done to them, which are strange like the parables that are struck.

﴿And they had plotted their plot﴾ in which they exhausted their effort to nullify the truth and establish falsehood. ﴿And with Allah is their plot﴾ meaning their deed is recorded with Him, so He will requite them for it; or with Him is that which will counter their plot as recompense for their scheming and to nullify it. ﴿And though their plot was﴾ in magnitude and severity ﴿such that the mountains might be moved thereby﴾ meaning it was intended to remove the mountains. It has been said that in is negative and the lam is emphatic for it, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah would not punish them﴾; and that the mountains are a parable for the matter of the Prophet ﷺ and the like. It has also been said that the particle is light (mukhaffafah) from the heavy (thaqilah), and the meaning is that they plotted in order to remove what is like firm mountains in steadfastness and establishment, namely the signs of Allah the Exalted and His laws. Al-Kisa'i read (la-tazulu) with a fatha and a raf', taking it as the light particle with the lam being the separating lam, and its meaning is the magnifying of their plot. It was also read with a fatha and a nasb, according to the dialect of those who open the lam of kay; and it was read: "in kada makruhum" (though their plot nearly...).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 47:

﴿So do not think that Allah would break His promise to His messengers﴾ like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We surely help Our messengers﴾, and ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾. Its original form is "mukhlifun rusulahu wa'dahu" (breaking His messengers' promise), but He placed the second object first, to signal that He does not break promises at all, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not break the appointment﴾. And if He does not break His promise to anyone, how would He break it to His messengers? ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty﴾, victorious, who cannot be deceived, capable, who cannot be resisted. ﴿Owner of retribution﴾ on behalf of His allies against His enemies.

﴿يَوْمَ تُبَدَّلُ الأرْضُ غَيْرَ الأرْضِ﴾ [On the Day the earth will be changed into a different earth] is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for ﴿يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمُ﴾ [the Day it comes to them], or an adverbial complement (*zarf*) for *al-intiqam* (retribution), or it is governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* (remember), or by ﴿لا يُخْلِفُ وعْدَهُ﴾ [He does not fail His promise]. It cannot be governed by *mukhlif* (one who fails), because what precedes *la* (not) cannot operate on what follows it. ﴿والسَّماواتُ﴾ [and the heavens] is conjoined (*ʿutifa*) to "the earth," and its implied form is "and the heavens [will be changed into] other than the heavens." Substitution (*tabdil*) may occur in the essence, as when you say, "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars," and to this refers His saying: ﴿بَدَّلْناهم جُلُودًا غَيْرَها﴾ [We will replace their skins with other skins]. It may also occur in the attribute, as when you say, "I changed the ring into a seal ring," by melting it and altering its shape, and to this refers His saying: ﴿يُبَدِّلُ اللَّهُ سَيِّئاتِهِمْ حَسَناتٍ﴾ [Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds]. The verse admits both meanings. On the authority of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: the earth will be changed into earth of silver, and the heavens into heavens of gold. On the authority of Ibn Masʿud and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them both: people will be gathered upon a white earth on which no one has committed a sin. On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: it is that same earth, but its attributes are changed. This is supported by what Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The earth will be changed into a different earth, and it will be spread out and stretched like a tanned leather (*adim ʿukaziyy*)." ﴿لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا ولا أمْتًا﴾ [in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness].

Know that on the first interpretation it does not necessarily follow that what results from the change is literally an earth and a heaven. On the second, it is not far-fetched that Allah makes the earth into Hell and the heavens into Paradise, as indicated by His saying: ﴿كَلا إنَّ كِتابَ الأبْرارِ لَفي عِلِّيِّينَ﴾ [No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin] and His saying: ﴿إنَّ كِتابَ الفُجّارِ لَفي سِجِّينٍ﴾ [Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin].

﴿وَبَرَزُوا﴾ [And they will come forth] from their graves ﴿لِلَّهِ الواحِدِ القَهّارِ﴾ [before Allah, the One, the Subduer], for His reckoning and recompense. Describing Him with these two attributes indicates that the matter is extremely severe, like His saying: ﴿لِمَنِ المُلْكُ اليَوْمَ لِلَّهِ الواحِدِ القَهّارِ﴾ [To whom belongs dominion today? To Allah, the One, the Subduer] (p-204). For when the matter belongs to One who overpowers and cannot be overpowered, there is no one to seek help from besides Him, nor any to seek refuge with.

﴿And you will see the criminals that Day bound together﴾. They are joined with one another according to their sharing in beliefs and deeds, as in His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ (81:7). Or they are joined with the devils, or with what they acquired of misguided beliefs and corrupt dispositions. Or ﴿their hands and their feet are joined to their necks with shackles﴾. This may be a figurative image of their being held to account for what their hands and feet committed.

﴿in the shackles﴾ (al-asfad) is connected to ﴿bound together﴾, or is a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring to its pronoun. Al-safad (شدّ / قيد) means a fetter. It is said that it means the iron collar (al-ghull). Salamah ibn Jandal said:

*And Zayd al-Khayl has met with shackles, biting on a forearm and a shin-bone.*

Its root meaning is binding.

﴿their shirts﴾ (sarabil) means their garments. ﴿of tar﴾ (qatiran). The word qatran has also come as a second dialectal form (lughatan) for it. It is the resin that exudes from the al-abhal tree (a kind of juniper), which is boiled, and with which mangy camels are smeared, so that its sharpness burns off the mange. It is black, foul-smelling, and catches fire quickly. The skins of the people of the Fire are smeared with it until its coating becomes for them like shirts, so that the sting of the tar, the ugliness of its color, the stench of its smell, and the swift spread of the fire on their skins all gather upon them. Yet the difference between these two tars is like the difference between these two fires. It may also be a figurative image of the wicked dispositions and savage states that surround the essence of the soul, bringing upon it all kinds of griefs and pains.

It is reported from Ya'qub (ibn Ishaq al-Hadrami, a Qur'an reader) that he read ﴿qitran﴾ (with a short vowel on the qaf). Al-qitr means copper, or molten brass, and "al-aniyy" means the vessel whose heat has reached its extreme. The clause is a second circumstantial phrase (hal thaniyah), or a circumstantial phrase referring to the pronoun in ﴿bound together﴾.

﴿and the Fire covers their faces﴾, that is, it envelops them, because they did not turn toward the truth with them, and did not use, in reflecting upon it, their perceptions and senses for which they were created. Just as it looks into their hearts, because they are empty of knowledge and filled with ignorance. ﴿That He may recompense every soul﴾ — i.e., He does that to them so that He may recompense every guilty soul. ﴿for what it has earned﴾. Or "every soul" means every soul, whether guilty or obedient (min mujrimatin aw muti'atin). For when He has shown that the guilty are punished for their guilt, it becomes known that the obedient are rewarded for their obedience; and this is what is required by attaching the lam (of purpose) to (barazu, "they came forth"). ﴿Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ — because no reckoning preoccupies Him from another reckoning.

**"This"** is a reference to the Qur'an, or to the surah, or to what it contains of admonition and reminder, or to what was described in His words: **﴿And do not think that Allah...﴾**.

**﴿A message for mankind﴾** means a sufficiency for them in admonition. **﴿And that they may be warned thereby﴾** is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to an elided clause, meaning: *that they may be advised, and that they may be warned by this message*. In that case the lām (*li-*) is attached to *balāgh* (message). It is also permissible for it to be attached to an elided clause, whose estimate is: *and that they may be warned thereby, by its being sent down or recited*. It has also been read with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, from *nadhara bihi* (*نَذَرَ بِهِ*), meaning he knew it and prepared himself for it.

**﴿And that they may know that He is only one God﴾**, through reflection and contemplation on the signs in it that point to Him, or that alert to what points to Him. **﴿And that people of understanding may take heed﴾**, so that they withdraw from what would destroy them and clothe themselves with what would bring them favor.

Know that He, glorified and exalted, mentioned three benefits of this message, which are the purpose and wisdom in sending down the Books: the perfecting of the messengers for the people; the completion of the theoretical faculty (*al-quwwa al-naẓariyya*, the faculty of reasoning and belief), whose ultimate perfection is *tawḥīd* (affirmation of God's oneness); and the rectification of the practical faculty (*al-quwwa al-ʿamaliyya*, the faculty of action), which is clothing oneself with the garment of *taqwā* (God-consciousness). May Allah, exalted be He, make us among those who attain both of them.

And it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Ibrahim will be given, as a reward, ten good deeds for each person who worshipped idols and for each person who did not worship them."
